text.p: *AUD off slightly after choppy night as market pondered the outlook for policy now the long awaited cut to 5.0 pct was over
*General feeling is the easing was last of cycle but another could not be ruled out if the data showed no growth pickup
*Analysts disappointed the rally did not follow through past $0.7475 and saw risk of $0.7420 being tested near term
By 8.15 am (2215 GMT) the currency was prevaricating at US$0.7435/40 having finished at US$0.7462/67 Tuesday after a bounce from an early US$0.7395 low.
A break of US$0.7420 would suggest the four month old downtrend had further yet to run and strong support at US$0.7330 could be called upon once again.

A breach of US$0.7530 -- which marks a 38 pecent retracement of the fall from the US$0.7890 peak in May to the recent 18-month low of US$0.7310 -- was needed to keep confidence in the recovery alive. On the wide, US$0.7070 remained the big target for bears while bulls were eyeing US$0.7650.

Dollar bulls had hoped the cut in official rates to 5.0 percent would be considered the last in the cycle, but some analysts were still holding out the prospect of another should data prove softer over the next few months.
The futures market reflected the risk with the 90-day bank bill contract for December up around 15 basis points since Wednesday morning to 95.12, implying a rate of 4.88 percent.

Until this matter was settled definitively the dollar would find it hard to sustain a rally above 75 cents. Today's retail sales figures for June had been rather pre-empted by the easing but would still provide a useful reading of consumer confidence.

Median forecasts are for sales to rise 0.4 percent on the month, a firm result given the hefty 2.9 percent gain recorded in May. However, real sales for Q2 would still only be up around 0.1 percent implying little or no contribution to GDP from consumer spending.

Treasurer Peter Costello gives a speech at an economist lunch around 12.30 pm and is likely to take an upbeat view on the economy and remind everyone that the full impact of past rate cuts has yet to show through.
Elsewhere, base metals turned lower and helped put a halt to a rally in the CRB index. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
